rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The intermediate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient slope while keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to identify which crowded pairs respond to slope. This should spread the central cluster and clarify whether temperature changes will be needed.
Keep the shallower gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity of the remaining close pair. Higher temperature should also reduce the last-peak time and its score penalty.

Test an intermediate temperature to avoid the co-elutions seen at 40 and 60 C while retaining the favorable shallow-gradient separation. If all pairs resolve, the next step will be to shorten retention slightly to remove the time penalty.

At 60 C only one pair remains unresolved, and all peaks elute before 10 minutes. Modestly steepen the gradient to test whether that co-elution separates while preserving resolution in the earlier cluster.

The unresolved pair improved as the gradient shortened from 24 to 22 minutes; shortening to 18 minutes should move it closer to baseline resolution. This also tests whether the earlier cluster retains sufficient resolution as the gradient steepens.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to lift the R = 1.46 pair above the target while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes. Monitor the later R = 1.64 pair, which may lose resolution as the slope decreases.

Keep the slope of injection 6 but shift the solvent window upward to test starting-composition selectivity, since slope changes alone trade resolution between two critical pairs. The first peak appears sufficiently retained to tolerate this modest increase in starting organic fraction.

Make the gradient slightly shallower than injection 8 to improve both early critical pairs while using its extra resolution margin in the later pair. The narrower solvent window still extends beyond the observed elution window and should keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the marginal early pairs above R = 1.5 while preserving the later pair’s margin. The final organic fraction remains above the last peak’s estimated elution composition, with ample time margin below 10 minutes.

Injection 10 achieves the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention, with the resulting shallower slope potentially compensating for compression of the early critical pairs.

Retain injection 10 as the maximum-score benchmark and explore lower-temperature selectivity for a potentially faster fully resolved method. A steeper gradient will counter the increased retention at 25 C while testing a substantially different separation pattern.

Shorten the low-temperature gradient to test whether the central co-elution responds to slope and whether a faster fully resolved separation is possible. Injection 10 remains the maximum-CRF benchmark.

Further steepen the low-temperature gradient to determine whether the central pair can reach baseline resolution in a substantially shorter run. The later close pair may worsen, so this also establishes whether temperature or starting composition must provide the remaining selectivity.
Keep the fast gradient fixed and raise temperature by one step to test whether selectivity improves the three marginal pairs. Injection 10 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score fallback.

Test a shallower gradient at 30 C, seeking separation on the opposite side of the central pair’s slope-dependent crossover. This temperature improved the late pair, and the last peak should still remain below 10 minutes.

Return to 60 C and test whether a higher starting organic fraction combined with a shallower gradient can yield a shorter fully resolved separation. Injection 10 remains the maximum-score benchmark; this run probes whether slope adjustment can recover the early-pair resolution lost at higher starting organic.

Test a narrower, higher-starting solvent window at 25 C, using a shallow slope to move beyond the central co-elution observed in the low-temperature scouting runs. This explores an alternative selectivity region while retaining injection 10 as the maximum-score method.

Lengthen injection 18’s gradient to spread its sole unresolved pair, while keeping temperature and endpoints fixed. The last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes, potentially providing another maximum-score method with different selectivity.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten the fully resolved low-temperature method. The simultaneously shallower slope may preserve the central pair’s resolution; injection 10 remains the faster maximum-score benchmark.

Raise temperature one step while holding injection 20’s gradient fixed to test whether the sole unresolved pair gains selectivity. This should also shorten retention, while the other pairs have useful resolution margins.

Lengthen the gradient by one step to improve the central pair, whose resolution barely changed with temperature. Monitor its neighboring pair and the final pair for losses as the slope decreases; injection 10 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Lower temperature to restore the final pair’s resolution while retaining the shallower gradient that resolved the central pair. The earlier temperature comparison suggests the central pair is relatively temperature-insensitive, and the last peak should remain below 10 minutes.

Test a shorter, narrower gradient near the fastest maximum-score method, injection 10. Its slightly shallower slope should improve the early critical pairs, but the later pair may fall below R = 1.5, defining the local limit.

Test a shallower slope at the higher starting composition to recover the early-pair resolution lost in injection 11 while seeking a shorter fully resolved separation. Injection 10 remains the preferred demonstrated method, with maximum CRF and the shortest last-peak time among fully resolved runs.
